analysis.one_liner: Cuts estate and gift tax rates and shields $10 million per person from the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote, after being folded into the larger 2001 tax cut bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the top rate on estate and gift taxes to 30 percent, let each person pass $10 million to heirs tax-free (with the amount rising with inflation), and let anyone give away $50,000 per year per recipient with no tax. It was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and was sent to the House tax-writing committee, which never acted on it. The record shows it was instead 'seen' into H.R. 1836, the large 2001 tax cut law that phased out the estate tax on its own.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the gains would have gone almost entirely to heirs of very large estates — the small share of families owing any estate tax at all under the rules of 2001. Wealthy individuals planning large lifetime gifts would also have gained from the higher annual gift exclusion, and families would have paid less to estate-planning professionals.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated estate tax rate schedule with a flat 30 percent rate, cutting taxes on the largest taxable estates [S3].
Raises the amount each person could pass to heirs tax-free to $10 million, indexed to inflation, up from roughly $675,000 in effect at introduction [S3].
Raises the annual tax-free gift exclusion from $10,000 to $50,000 per recipient, letting wealthy individuals transfer far more to relatives during their lifetimes without tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Estate and gift taxes are paid by a small number of very wealthy families, so cutting them reduces revenue collected from the top of the income and wealth distribution; the difference would have been made up through other taxes, borrowing, or lower spending.

drawbacks.text: The tax cuts would have reduced federal revenue, a cost borne by taxpayers collectively; the bill contains no offsetting revenue [S3].

The benefit is concentrated at the very top: in 2001 only estates above roughly $675,000 owed any estate tax, so the $10 million exclusion and the rate cut primarily serve the largest estates, not ordinary families [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would have gone almost entirely to heirs of the largest estates, while its costs were spread across all taxpayers through lost revenue. Because only a tiny fraction of estates owed any estate tax in 2001, the bill offered little or nothing to most families, and its design (a $10 million per-person exemption plus a higher annual gift exclusion) was squarely aimed at large fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House tax-writing committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 8, 2001, with no cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee [S1][S4][S5].
The committee took no recorded action on the bill; it was never marked up or voted on [S5].
On August 13, 2001, the record notes 'See H.R. 1836,' the broad 2001 tax cut law, which addressed the estate tax separately and phased it down over several years [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal revenue from estate and gift taxes was preserved for the moment, while heirs of the largest estates still gained a phase-down of the estate tax through H.R. 1836, the larger 2001 tax cut law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large-estate heirs, via the broader 2001 tax cut

for.name: Rep. James A. Leach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut estate and gift tax rates and raise exemptions; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; it had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded opposition or support in committee.

industries.industry: Heirs and owners of very large estates
industries.note: The bill would have let each person pass $10 million tax-free and taxed estates at a flat 30 percent, a cut paid for by foregone federal revenue from the wealthiest families. In 2001 only estates above roughly $675,000 owed the tax at all, so ordinary families were unaffected directly either way [S3].

industries.industry: Estate planning, trusts, and wealth management services
industries.note: A larger exemption and higher annual gift exclusion reduce the need for estate-planning work and for insurance products sold to cover estate tax bills. This is a narrow professional-services loss, not a burden on working families.
